images.text:
Peter: Hi, Paula! Did you finish cleaning the house yesterday?
Paula: I started, but I haven't finished yet. How are you?
Peter: I'm so disappointed. I haven't heard the end of your parents' story yet.
Paula: OK, so you want to know more?
Peter: Absolutely! I've been wanting to know how it ends since you started.
Paula: Well ... where were we? I've been telling this story a lot lately.

Peter: Your mother was sending letters to your uncle to learn about your father's life.
Paula: Oh, yes. Well, in one of the letters, she learned that my father had a new girlfriend.
Peter: She must have felt so sad!
Paula: Yes, she was devastated. In fact, she has always been a very strong-willed woman. She decided that she had to go back to Italy before the new relationship turned into something serious.
Peter: That sounds very gutsy.
Paula: Yes, but it was better than staying at home and crying your heart out. Have you ever heard of someone being so smitten?

Peter: What was her plan?
Paula: She didn't want to lie to her parents, so she told them she had business in Milan for a few days. Of course, they thought she meant Milan, New York, a city about 20 minutes away. Really, she meant Milan, Italy. She packed a suitcase and bought a one-way ticket at the airport.
Peter: I wish I had that much courage.
Paula: I wish I did, too.

Present Perfect Continuous vs. Present Perfect
You use these tenses  to express that an action began in the past and is still going on or has just finished.
You use the Present Perfect tense mainly to express that an action is completed or to emphasize the result.
Forms:
Regular verbs: form of 'have' + base form of verb + ed
Example: I haven't finished cleaning yet.
Irregular verbs: form of 'have' + past participle of irregular verbs
Example: I haven't heard the end of the story yet.
You use the Present Perfect Continuous tense to emphasize the duration or continuous course of an action.
Form:
Form of 'have' + been + base form of verb + ing
Example: I've been telling this story a lot lately.

Show you understand someone's feelings or situation

It is common to show you understand someone's feelings in a conversation.
You use “I wish ...” to talk about things you do not have or do, or you cannot have or do.
The verb wish introduces an idea. After wish, you use a verb in the past tense.

I wish I knew ...
I wish I had ...
I wish you were ...

Structure:
Wish + Simple Past tense
Example:
I wish I had that much courage.
I wish I did, too.
Ann: Your mother was so brave to leave everything behind to be with the love of her life. She must have felt so sad to be apart from him.
Bob: I wish I had that much courage.
Ann: I wish I did, too.

Structure:
Modal + have+ past participle
You can use modals to show you understand someone's feelings in a past situation.
Example:
Your mother must have felt so sad.
devastated
shocked and overwhelmed; in grief
(adjective)
Example: She was devastated when she found out that my dad had a new girlfriend.
